claim: Bednarczyk, Omran, and Bayle derive passivity filters for variable impedance control that either screen a prescribed diagonal stiffness/damping transition or reshape its scalar switching variables so derived storage-function inequalities remain satisfied. A first filter follows a known conservative condition; a second introduces a time-varying filtered-error matrix and a new storage function to admit faster, less conservative stiffness changes. Conditional passivity is analytical for the continuous, diagonal, constant-virtual-mass model and implemented profile constraints. A one-dimensional simulation supports reduced conservatism of the second condition, and a KUKA iiwa needle-insertion demonstration shows the filter limiting the rate of a stiffness increase while penetrating a layered silicone phantom. The paper does not test human interaction, broad task performance, uncertainty robustness, or comprehensive safety, and its practical filter is itself a conservative approximation to a derivative-dependent condition.
epistemic_status: qualified primary analytical, simulation, and hardware-demonstration evidence: passivity follows for the explicitly modeled diagonal impedance and filter inequalities; reduced conservatism is illustrated in one scalar simulation, and experimental support is a single robot-phantom needle task without statistical comparison
problem_and_setting: Time-varying impedance can improve dexterity and adapt interaction to task or human state, but increasing stiffness may inject energy and destroy passivity. Existing conditions can determine offline whether a prescribed profile is passive but do not necessarily repair it, while energy tanks act online and depend on measured state and tank tuning. The paper seeks a profile-level filter usable offline or online that tracks a desired transition while enforcing passivity.
method_or_mechanism: After computed-torque linearization, the desired Cartesian error behavior uses constant diagonal virtual mass M and time-varying diagonal damping D(t) and stiffness K(t). Each parameter moves from an initial to final value through a diagonal switching matrix Gamma with scalar gamma_i in [0,1]. The first filter combines a low-pass tracking term beta(gamma_bar-gamma) with an upper bound on gamma_dot derived from the established storage function V2. To reduce conservatism, the paper replaces the constant filtered-error coefficient with a bounded time-dependent diagonal matrix B, derives storage V3, then sets B=D and defines V4. The resulting conditions involve D_dot, D_ddot, and K_dot. Because the direct bound would require differentiating a discontinuous min-switch output, a more conservative implementable rate limit h3 is substituted, yielding gamma_dot=min(h2,h3,beta(gamma_bar-gamma)).
content_summary: The analysis begins with the standard variable mass-damper-spring error model and shows why the conventional kinetic-plus-stiffness storage cannot certify increasing stiffness. A filtered tracking-error storage gives two known matrix inequalities and a first scalar passivity filter. A generalized filtered error and Schur-complement argument lead to a second family of inequalities and a practical second filter. In a scalar simulation with mass 10 kg, stiffness 2 to 22 N/m, damping ratio 0.1, sinusoidal reference, and beta=10, the V4-based switching profile reaches its desired value faster than the V2-based profile while the corresponding storage derivative remains nonpositive. Hardware validation uses a KUKA iiwa 14 with an ATI Mini40 sensor and a 16G needle entering a four-layer silicone phantom. Translational stiffness is scheduled by material, virtual inertial terms are 5 kg, damping ratio is 1, beta=50, and control runs at 500 Hz. At skin puncture around 9.35 s, the filter constrains the change from 1000 to 3500 N/m.
synthesis_role: Provides a deterministic profile-shaping alternative to energy tanks and complementary-force MPC. It is useful when a desired gain transition is known in advance or generated online and can be restricted to the paper's diagonal interpolation form, but its guarantee does not cover arbitrary matrix-valued adaptation or implementation uncertainty.
development_link: The paper builds directly on Kronander and Billard's variable-impedance passivity inequalities, converting them into an explicit repair filter, and develops a less conservative storage function. Later PMPIC work compares against this filter and seeks to preserve the original stiffness profile by adding an optimized complementary force instead of changing gains.

evidence.finding: For constant diagonal mass and time-varying diagonal damping/stiffness, a filtered-error storage function yields sufficient passivity inequalities; increasing stiffness is the relevant energy-injection case.
A scalar interpolation of each diagonal impedance term is rate-limited by the sufficient condition and combined with low-pass reference tracking to form the first passivity filter.
A time-dependent diagonal filtered-error matrix yields a new positive storage construction and sufficient inequalities involving the derivatives of damping and stiffness.
The exact condition contains gamma_ddot; the practical filter substitutes a more conservative rate bound h3 and takes the minimum of passivity and tracking limits.
The V4-based filter follows the desired switching profile faster than the V2-based filter in one configured mass-spring-damper example while its selected storage derivative stays nonpositive.
During layered-phantom needle insertion, the KUKA iiwa implementation at 500 Hz constrains the switching-variable rate when stiffness rises from 1000 to 3500 N/m at skin puncture.
The authors seek less conservative conditions and identify unusual transitions, such as increasing stiffness while decreasing damping, as requiring further investigation.

boundary_conditions: Virtual mass is constant; mass variation is outside the derivation.
Mass, damping, stiffness, and switching matrices are chosen diagonal so the analysis decouples by Cartesian coordinate.
The principal construction assumes stiffness increases and damping does not decrease; singular or opposing parameter changes require separate numerical handling.
Passivity is with respect to the filtered error r and external force under computed-torque linearization, not a direct guarantee of bounded contact force or human injury prevention.
The practical V4 filter uses a deliberately conservative replacement for a condition involving the second derivative of the switching variable.
The experimental result is one needle and one layered silicone phantom on one robot, with no human subjects, comparator trials, uncertainty analysis, or statistical outcomes.
The derivation is continuous-time; a 500 Hz implementation is reported without a sampled-data passivity proof.
Model error, torque saturation, friction-compensation error, sensor noise, delay, and coupled rotational adaptation are not part of the guarantee.
assumptions: Computed-torque control realizes the stated Cartesian impedance model closely enough for the derived storage inequalities to apply.
Desired and initial/final impedance matrices are symmetric positive definite and diagonal, with bounded positive damping.
Each switching variable remains in [0,1], is sufficiently differentiable where required, and follows the implemented min-based differential equation.
The filtered-error coefficient or matrix remains positive and bounded so bounded r implies bounded position and velocity error.
The selected filter rate beta and gain profiles are feasible at the implementation sample rate.
The environment is passive when passivity is used to infer coupled stability.

reported: Arbitrary time variation, especially increasing stiffness, can destroy passivity of otherwise passive fixed impedance control.
The earlier V2 condition can be conservative and delay tracking of the desired switching profile.
The direct V4-derived filter is impractical because it requires differentiating a potentially discontinuous min-switch output.
The implementable filter therefore adopts a more conservative bound.
Increasing stiffness while decreasing damping can create singular or more restrictive cases and is left for further investigation.
inferred: Rapid or coupled full-matrix impedance adaptations may not be representable by independent scalar switching variables.
Numerical differentiation, sensor noise, discretization, and rate saturation can violate the continuous inequalities at hardware level.
A filter can preserve passivity by slowing a clinically or task-critical stiffness change so much that task performance degrades.
The phantom demonstration shows implementability but cannot establish safety or effectiveness in real tissue or physical human-robot interaction.
